learnerStatement: Simulated learner. This review finds problems; it is not evidence that anyone learned.
learnerBoundary: Everyday numeracy, simple charts, comparison of numbers and familiar household objects; no domain-specific theory assumed.

observations.prediction: Selected 180 degrees and locked it in.
observations.exploration: Initial explored 30 E gave sum 210, excess 30 and 4.2 percent Earth. Right step 60 E gave 240, excess 60 and 8.3 percent. At 90 E sum 270 and 12.5 percent with three visible right-angle labels. End 150 E gave 330 and 20.8 percent. Home restored 30 E.
observations.reveal: Corrected to 270 for the asked 90 E triangle, explained flat versus spherical geometry, related excess to area and used retained observations 30 and 90 degrees excess. Tiny triangles have negligible excess was stated.
observations.visual: Actual dark 1257 by 936 screenshots inspected. At 90 E three 90-degree labels and shaded spherical triangle visible. Reveal inner scroll clipped pole/top of current 30 E triangle, while metrics, history and explanation were readable.
observations.previewIsolation: Preview banner said history and analytics are not saved.
observations.blinding: No source, builder notes or other reviews inspected.

prediction.reason: A familiar rule is tested in a concretely different surface setting.

interaction.reason: Discrete corner changes expose linked angle and area measures reversibly.

payoff.reason: Reveal explains the counterexample and numerical area relation.
payoff.evidence: Three right angles and one-eighth Earth at 90 E.

clarity.reason: Angle labels and history are strong; spherical side definition is implicit and reveal clips top.
clarity.evidence: Meridians and equator drawn; no explicit great-circle-side definition in visible explanation.

transfer.reason: Tiny-triangle approximation and excess principle are explained without a fresh application.

accessibility.evidence: Keyboard slider worked; screen reader, contrast and reduced motion unaudited.

surprise.reason: Three right angles violate the familiar flat triangle total.

visualExplanation.reason: Globe and shaded region show surface dependence.
visualExplanation.evidence: Corner angles and area change together.

playfulness.reason: Dragging a globe corner changes geometry.

practicalValue.reason: Clarifies limits of school geometry at global scales.

depth.evidence: One degree excess equals one seven-hundred-twentieth Earth.

complexity.reason: One slider supports a substantial shift from flat to spherical reasoning.
complexity.conceptualDemand: Distinguish surface geometry and relate angular excess to enclosed area.
complexity.interfaceBurden: Single stepped slider with trial history; inner scroll at reveal.
complexity.prerequisiteNovelty: Spherical triangle and excess introduced through globe.
complexity.notationRepresentationBurden: Longitude, degrees, area percentages and fraction of Earth.

whyCool: A triangle can have three right angles when its sides follow a curved world.
caveat: Great-circle-side condition is visually implicit; reveal scroll clips the pole at the tested position.
effort: Approximately 3 minutes of actual browser review.
